lesson.title: From Problem to Plan: Designing Algorithms Before You Code
lesson.summary: Algorithm design is the process of planning a correct, step-by-step solution in plain language or pseudocode before translating it into code.
lesson.body:
You already know that an algorithm is a finite sequence of steps that solves a problem. Algorithm design is what happens before any of those steps get written as code: it is the process of planning a clear, correct sequence of steps in plain language or pseudocode first, and only translating that plan into a specific programming language once you are confident the logic itself is right.

This matters because writing code and designing logic are two different kinds of thinking, and doing them at the same time makes both harder. If you try to work out the solution to a problem while also fighting Python syntax, indentation, and variable naming, a mistake in your logic and a mistake in your syntax look identical: your program just does not work, and you cannot easily tell which kind of problem you are looking at. Planning the algorithm first, separately from the code, lets you evaluate whether the logic itself is correct, using nothing more than a concrete example and your own reasoning, the same way you traced code by hand in an earlier chapter, but now applied to a plan you have not yet written as code at all.

A reasonable design process looks like this. Restate the problem clearly enough that you could explain it to someone else. Identify exactly what the inputs and outputs are. Work through at least one concrete example by hand, computing the answer yourself, so you have something to check your eventual code against. Write the steps out as pseudocode or a numbered list, not yet in any particular language. Deliberately think through edge cases, such as an empty input or an input with only one item, before you write a single line of real code. Only then translate the plan into your programming language.

As an example, consider designing an algorithm to find the second largest number in a list of distinct numbers, without sorting the whole list first. Restate the problem: given a list, return the number that is smaller than the maximum but larger than every other number. Work an example by hand: for [7, 2, 9, 4], the largest is 9 and the second largest is 7. Design a plan: scan the list once, keeping track of two values, the largest seen so far and the second largest seen so far. For each number, if it is larger than the current largest, the old largest becomes the new second largest, and this number becomes the new largest; otherwise, if it is larger than the current second largest, it becomes the new second largest. Trace the plan against the example before coding it: starting with largest and second_largest both set very low, 7 becomes the new largest; 2 is not larger than 7, but is larger than the placeholder second largest, so it becomes the new second largest; 9 is larger than 7, so 7 becomes the new second largest and 9 becomes the new largest; 4 is not larger than 9 and not larger than 7, so nothing changes. The result is largest equal to 9 and second_largest equal to 7, which matches the hand computed answer.

Only after this plan is confirmed correct, by hand, on paper, does it make sense to write it as actual code. This also surfaces edge cases worth deciding on deliberately, such as what should happen if the list has fewer than two elements, or if the largest value appears more than once, before those cases show up as confusing bugs discovered by accident later. Designing the algorithm first turns those into design decisions made on purpose, instead of bugs found by luck.
